title: Overhaul GLES3 shader compiler
body:
Further help for https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/86731

This PR is split into 3 commits since each commit does a very different optimization. I figured it was best this way to make it easier to review and bisect regressions

### Background

<details>

<summary>Not necessary, but good info for reference if you want to learn more</summary>

Our shader system is built around 3 concepts:
1. Shader versions: the set of code and render modes that come from the user
2. Shader variants: A set of defines that are always compiled when the shader is first used that enable/disable features
3. Specializations: A more fine-tuned set of defines that are used to fully optimize the shader for performance

The goal was that Shader variants would be used for things that require changing shader inputs/outputs (i.e. they change the overall shape of the shader). While specializations would be used for micro-optimizations. Therefore, running a shader with a different specialization should be completely valid, it would just be slower. The default variants would fall back on the default specialization state whenever a specialization wasn't available. 

This is an ubershader-like design except there are no run time uniform branches, everything is static. 

Unfortunately, this design never worked out as we planned. Very quickly I found that compile time was prohibitive if everything that changed inputs/outputs was made into a variant. We had a variant explosion due to all the combinations. Likewise, the original design assumed that we would use a lot of uniform branching, but that kills performance on lower end devices, so a lot of things ended up as Specializations. 

In the end, we found a balance that was okay, but didn't really work well to reduce compile times. We paid the cost of the variants on every shader version even if the default specialization would never be used in practice. This had the effect of making the first shader compilation at least 5x more expensive than necessary. I say "at least" because the default specialization included most features, so each of those compilations was more expensive than a typical compilation. 

Even if the default specialization was used, we still paid the cost of:
1. The depth mode even if the depth prepass was disabled (this is just wasted time)
2. The instanced mode even if that shader was never used on a multimesh.

So, even in the case of the needed specialization matching the default specialization, the cost could still be 4x higher than necessary (typically it would only be 2x higher since we often need the depth variant).

We gave up on this system for the canvas shader in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/87553 and https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/87558 since compile time was so painful. 

Overall, this design has caused us to compiler way more shaders than necessary. So it seems like it is time to let it go. 

</details>

### Introduction

I started out attempting to apply similar optimizations to those I did in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/87553 and https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/87558. Namely, reduce the number of variants so we don't pay the cost of compiling a bunch of unused variants (this is what the third commit ended up being). 

However, when profiling in Superluminal, I noticed that a lot of the cost in compiling shaders wasn't in the driver at all. Which led me to the first commit. Optimizing the shader builder (more on this below).

I then noticed that the majority of remaining time was spent waiting for shader linking (when not using cache), or waiting on glProgramBinary (when using cache). Which made me realize that, upon loading a shader for the first time, we are loading all program binaries and re-linking the shader for every permutation that we have seen of that shader. This ends up costing a lot of time for shaders that never get used. This problem is even worse because of the fact that we precompile a bunch of variants with the default specialization that are never used (I explain this in more detail in the background above). This led to the second commit where I optimized our shader caching strategy.

Ultimately, the three commits overlap, since commit 3 allows us to compile fewer variants, the cost of building the strings and caching the shaders goes down. Therefore, the relative benefit of each is hard to capture since the speed boost will change depending on the order I apply the commits. At any rate, there is a nice improvement at each stage. So I think all three are worth merging

### Performance

So far I have tested with my synthetic benchmark using a dev build on my main development machine on Linux (AMD Ryzen 9 8945HS w/ Radeon 780M Graphics)

Found here: [ShaderCompilationIssue2.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33582300/ShaderCompilationIssue2.zip)

**Dev build**
|          | 2D     | 2D no cache | 3D     | 3D no cache |
|----------|--------|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Master   | 130 ms | 300 ms      | 450 ms | 1600 ms     |
| Strings  | 130 ms | 145 ms      | 450 ms | 600 ms      |
| Cache    | 130 ms | 145 ms      | 110 ms | 600 ms      |
| Variants | 130 ms | 145 ms      | 90 ms  | 160 ms      |

**Optimized build**

|          | 2D    | 2D no cache | 3D     | 3D no cache |
|----------|-------|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Master   | 45 ms | 110 ms      | 420 ms | 890 ms      |
| Strings  | 45 ms | 70 ms       | 420 ms | 600 ms      |
| Cache    | 45 ms | 70 ms       | 75 ms  | 600 ms      |
| Variants | 45 ms | 70 ms       | 50 ms  | 130 ms      |

I expected there to be less benefit on optimized builds (and there was), but there is still a nice benefit from all the optimizations. Especially note how the first optimization brings both cases to 600 ms. At that point all the cost is in the driver, so compiler optimizations don't help. 

Note: I still need to do smoke testing on other platforms (particularly web and Android). However, I expect there to be similar gains on all platforms since most of these optimizations are in the category of "simply do less work".

### Commit 1: Shader Builder

This commit has two parts:
1. Fixed a bug where each line got treated as its own shader chunk. This caused a huge amount of duplicate work when assembly the shader. 
2. Switched away from StringBuilder to a custom approach. 

I would have preferred to use a template, but this situation is a bit unique. We need to avoid using String since CowData has a lot of overhead and we were spending too much time converting back and forth between String and utf8. 

### Commit 2: Shader Cache

This does a few things:
1. Split loading the shader cache file from creating pipelines
2. Don't save the entire cache every time we compile a new pipeline
4. Defer saving the pipeline cache until we exit the program
5. Only save the pipeline cache if we compile new specializations. 

This had a big benefit for the scene shader since it typically has several specializations per shader version. There was no measurable benefit in my test project for 2D since the canvas shader rarely has multiple specializations per version. 

As part of this change I also added the `GL_PROGRAM_BINARY_RETRIEVABLE_HINT`. I'm pretty sure it gets ignored on most devices. I didn't measure a performance benefit from using it. But I suspect it will help out in a few situations where the shader cache appears to not work. 

### Commit 3: Scene Shader Variants

Same rationale as https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/87553 and https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/87558. We are currently paying the cost of compiling 4 shader variants that never get used in practice. We can reduce that cost to just 1 shader variant. In other words, when you first encounter a shader, you compile 1 variant that is unlikely to be used, and 1 variant that you will use. 

I modified the default specialization to reduce the cost of that unused variant as much as possible. But it is still wasted work. 

Overall, I view this 3rd commit as a stopgap solution until we can do something better. In the long term, we need to do a heavier refactor of this system and actually use an ubershader. Then, when you first encounter a shader, you compile the ubershader and queue up compilation of the specialization in the background. 

### TODOS

- [ ] Add handling for Android application pause (need to save the cache on pause like in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/114463)
- [ ] Profile more projects and on more devices
- [ ] (Long term) We need to make an actual ubershader system :/ (I prototyped something, but this will be a lot of work)
